From left: the lane up from the harbour; the beach we had to ourselves on the last morning.

JUST BACK FROM

The Coast, in Four Days

We arrived after dark with one bag between three of us and no plan beyond the first night. The guesthouse was at the top of a lane so steep the taxi gave up halfway, and we walked the rest with the sea going silver below us.

The days found their own shape. Coffee on the step, a swim before the heat, a long lunch that turned into the afternoon. Nobody checked the time; the bells did that for us.

On the last morning we had the beach entirely to ourselves, and we stayed until the tide came up to our towels.

— YOUR NAME HERE

A BRIEF GUIDE TO
THE COAST

Where to stay: Up the hill, not on the front. The rooms are cheaper and the roof terraces catch the last of the light.

Where to eat: Wherever the tables spill into the street after nine. Order what the next table is having.

How to get around: On foot, mostly. A scooter for the far beaches; the bus if you are in no hurry at all.

What to pack: Less than you think, and shoes that can take a steep stone lane.

PASS IT ON

“Go the week after the crowds leave. The sea is still warm, and the town is yours again.”

pages.title: Letter home
pages.html:
The coast, a Thursday

Dear you,

I am writing this at a table that wobbles, outside a house covered in pots. Somebody here waters every one of them at seven each evening, and I have started timing my walk home to watch.

The town is steep and slow and entirely uninterested in hurrying for anybody. I have stopped checking the time. I have stopped, if I am honest, checking most things.

I wish you were here. Mostly so you could tell me I was right to come.

Yours, from the top of the lane — Your Name

pages.title: Drop-cap essay
pages.html:
ESSAY

On Going Slowly

In praise of the trip that refused to be efficient

BY YOUR NAME

There is a kind of travel that is really a list: see this, eat that, photograph the other, and move on before the light changes. We had done that kind before, and come home more tired than we left.

This time we tried the opposite. One town. No list. A rule that nobody was allowed to say “we should” before lunch. The first morning it felt like cheating; by the second it felt like the only sensible way to be anywhere.

What we found is that a place reveals itself in repetition. The first time you walk a lane you see the lane. The fourth time you see the woman who sweeps her step at nine, the cat that owns the third stair, the exact moment the shade reaches the café tables and everyone shifts their chairs six inches to the left.

None of it would make a list. All of it is what we talk about now.

Going slowly is not doing less. It is letting a place do more of the work, and being there, unhurried, when it does.

pages.title: Interview
pages.html:
Q&A · THE TRAVELLER

“I just kept walking uphill.”

Four days, one coast, and the case for never checking the map.

Why this coast?
Honestly, it was the cheapest place with a sea. Everything after that was luck.

The best meal?
A plate of something we never identified, at a café whose sign had been painted over.

And the gull?
It came to us. We simply did not say no.

What would you tell a friend going next?
Go the week after the crowds leave. Stay up the hill. Say yes to the second coffee.

Anything you would do differently?
Pack half. Stay twice as long. Wear better shoes for the lanes.

Going back?
We have not properly left yet.

pages.title: Opener
pages.html:
Feature

The Coast, in Four Days

Words and pictures — you

We arrived after dark with one bag between three of us and no plan beyond the first night. The guesthouse was at the top of a lane so steep the taxi gave up halfway, and we walked the rest with the sea going silver below us.

The owner met us at the gate with a torch and a plate of figs, as if we had been expected for years rather than booked the afternoon before. She showed us the roof, the kettle and the key, in that order, and went to bed.

The days found their own shape. Coffee on the step, a swim before the heat, a long lunch that turned into the afternoon. Nobody checked the time; the bells in the square did that for us, and they were not always right.

On the second morning we took the ferry across the bay. A gull followed it the whole way over, riding the wind a few feet above the rail, and by the time we landed it had a name and a small, loyal following among the children on board.

The town on the far side climbs straight out of the water. Every lane is a staircase, every staircase ends at a door painted a colour you would not choose for your own, and every door has a cat asleep in front of it.

We ate where the tables spilled into the street after nine, and ordered whatever the next table was having. It was usually fish, usually grilled, and always followed by something small and fierce in a glass that nobody could name.

The terrace walk was supposed to take an hour. It took three, most of them uphill, and at the top a man was selling lemonade from a cool box as though he had been waiting there all morning for exactly us.

Somewhere on the way down we stopped talking about home. It happens on every trip if you let it, the moment the place stops being somewhere you are visiting and becomes, for a few days, simply where you are.
